n3cs3w.title: ‘Hunger Games: Sunrise On The Reaping’ Heading To Potential Franchise-Record Monday With $12M
n3cs3w.content:
EXCLUSIVE: After scoring the best domestic opening weekend for Lionsgate in 12 years, The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping, could notch a Monday franchise record of $12M+.

The previous Monday record for the feature take of the Suzanne Collins’ novels belonged to 2013’s Catching Fire which did $12.3M. Seriously, Lionsgate resuscitated life back into this YA series after it hit an all-time low opening and result three years with The Hunger Games: Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes ($44.6M domestic opening, $166.3M North American take, $363.9M worldwide). The first Monday of Songbirds & Snakes came in at $5.2M.

If Sunrise of the Reaping‘s Monday eases below Catching Fire‘s, then it will wind up being the second best Monday in the franchise ahead of 2012’s The Hunger Games ($10.8M).

The fifth directed movie in the six-title franchise has enough mojo to lead throughout Thanksgiving per sources with a least $50M+, if not much more over the Wednesday through Sunday frame, well head of new openers, Universal/Paramount’s Focker-in-Law and Walt Disney Animation’s original movie Hexed, both at $45M apiece.

Sunrise on the Reaping came in a little lighter than the $120M forecasted with $119.3M, still the fourth best in the Lionsgate Collins canon after 2013’s Catching Fire ($70.9M Friday/previews, $158M 3-day), the first 2012 Hunger Games ($67.2M Friday/previews and $152.5M opening), and 2014’s Hunger Games: Mockingjay Part 1 ($55.1M Friday/previews and $121.8M 3-day). Catching Fire still owns the record as Lionsgate’s biggest opening ever at the North American box office.

Sunrise on the Reaping posted a $55.6M Friday (versus $56M reported yesterday, which included $21M previews), Saturday of $36.1M (versus $36.3M) and Sunday of $27.5M (versus $27.3M). The running cume through four days on the Joseph Zada, Mckenna Grace, Elle Fanning, Jesse Plemons, Ralph Fiennes and Kieran Culkin ensemble.

Before Sunrise on the Reaping, the last big opening for Lionsgate at the domestic box office was 2014’s The Hunger Games: Mockingjay Part 1.

1vq1ykl.title: Gram Parsons Estate Signs With Peermusic
1vq1ykl.content:
Peermusic has signed a publishing deal for the song catalog of Gram Parsons and will assume worldwide administration, it was announced last week by Peermusic CEO Mary Megan Peer and U.S./ Canada president Jamie Cerreta. Perhaps more than any other artist, Parsons — who was inducted posthumously into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame on November 14 — was responsible for the country-rock fusion that has spawned everything from the music of the Eagles to the entire Americana genre. His influence was obvious in a showcase held earlier this month at his old haunt, the Troubador in Los Angeles, featuring his musical collaborator Emmylou Harris, as well as Elvis Costello, the Black Crowes, and Margo Price.

Polly Parsons said: “My father’s music has always had a life of its own, reaching across generations and continuing to inspire artists and listeners in ways I don’t think even he could have imagined. It means so much to me to help preserve that legacy while also finding new ways for people to discover his songs. His music was never bound by genre or convention, and I think that’s why it still resonates so deeply today. My hope is that this new partnership will not only honor the incredible body of work he left behind but also introduce his music to a whole new generation of fans. Keeping his spirit and his songs alive is something I hold very close to my heart.”

Jamie Cerreta commented: “Gram’s music is an enduring testament to how great songs remain in our hearts. All of us at Peermusic are so honored to represent his songs and to see his work celebrated through his recent induction into the Rock n Roll Hall of Fame. I am personally so happy to be working with Polly and Vector Management to help another generation discover the greatness of Gram Parsons.”

+ The Songwriters Hall of Fame has announced the posthumous induction of legendary singer-songwriter Roger Miller, known for such hits at “King of the Road” and “Dang Me.” Miller, who died in 1992 at age 56, was honored during an intimate ceremony held November 17, 2026, at BMI headquarters on Music Row in Nashville.

Miller’s widow Mary said: “We were ecstatic to learn that Roger was being inducted into the Songwriters Hall of Fame. Of all his many talents, he was most proud of his songwriting. This lifetime achievement would have meant a great deal to him, and we are honored to celebrate the recognition of his extraordinary body of work.”

+ Ignacio Meyer has been named president of Universal Music Latin America & Iberian Peninsula, effective immediately. He will report to Felipe Holguin, who was named CEO of the division last week. Meyer has held leadership roles at TelevisaUnivision since 2011. Most recently he was president of its U.S. Networks & Local Media; previously, he founded and served as managing partner of advisory firm Konexxion Enterprises, worked as an artist manager and served on the management team of IFPI Latin America.

Holguin said: “Artists are at the heart of how we’re building this next chapter. Nacho combines creative sensibility and strategic vision with a deep understanding of how to nurture each artist’s individuality, grow their audience, and heighten their impact across platforms. He’ll add a powerful dimension to our leadership team as we invest in extraordinary artists and bring bold ideas to life. We know from experience how well we work together, and I’m delighted to welcome him to UMG.”

+ Americana award-winning artist Nathaniel Rateliff has signed with Red Light Management’s Will Botwin and Coran Capshaw for representation. Rateliff recently marked his 10th straight year performing at Farm Aid after being unanimously appointed to the Farm Aid board of directors; performed at Tom Morello’s inaugural Power to the People festival alongside Bruce Springsteen, Dave Matthews and Morello; and he closed this year’s Newport Folk Festival alongside Matthews, Joan Baez and more with his Nathaniel Rateliff & Friends set.

+ Warner Records has signed 21-year-old Brazilian-Mexican-American singer Lambb and released her second EP, “There’s Someone in the Yard,” last week. The singer, born Julie Gaeta, combines indie singer-songwriter approach with house and techno, and last summer performed at the Reading Festival and Leeds Festival in England as part of her first headlining tour.

+ Position Music has signed Grammy-nominated artist and songwriter Masego to a worldwide publishing deal. Masego recently released his third album, “Fix Your Face,” and was signed to Position Music by Delmar Powell, VP of A&R for the company.

“Masego is a generational creative talent and a true artist in every sense of the word. His ability to seamlessly blend jazz, R&B, hip-hop, and global influences has created a sound that is uniquely his own, while continuing to push the boundaries of Black music. Beyond his incredible gifts as a songwriter, producer, and musician, I genuinely believe there are few artists who can match what he brings to the stage,” said Delmar Powell, VP of A&R.

+ Sweden-based music investment firm Pophouse Entertainment has made two senior appointments to its leadership team: Kristina Heney joins as President, Commercial & Marketing, based in New York, and Greg Lombardo joins as President, Pophouse Avatar Network, based in Los Angeles. According to the announcement, the pair will play central roles in the continued growth of Pophouse’s brands, live experiences and productions, which include artists such as Kiss, Iron Maiden, Tina Turner, Sia, Cyndi Lauper and Avicii. Heney joins from Oak View Group, where she most recently served as EVP, Marketing, Media and Conferences. She was previously Chief Marketing & Experience Officer of Cirque du Soleil Entertainment Group, along with roles at Madison Square Garden Entertainment and the NBA’s Global Merchandising Group. Lombardo joins from Netflix, where he was VP and Global Head of Experiences. He was previously at 20th Century Fox and BRC Imagination Arts.

+ Litmus Music, a music rights investment and management business, has announced approximately $475 million in new capital commitments from global investment firm Carlyle and investment funds managed by KKR, a leading global investment firm, to support its continued growth and strategic acquisition opportunities. Carlyle Global Credit, which partnered with Litmus’s management team to establish the business in 2022, will retain a majority stake in the Company following the transaction. The platform’s portfolio includes over 100,000 copyrights and recordings, including music from globally recognized artists and songwriters including Katy Perry, benny blanco, Randy Newman, and Keith Urban.

“Together with Carlyle and our team, we’ve built Litmus into a scalable music rights management business rooted in trust, creativity, analysis and, above all, our passion for music,” said Hank Forsyth, Co-Founder and Chief Executive Officer of Litmus Music. “This investment marks an exciting next chapter for our company, providing meaningful additional capital to pursue new deals and accelerate growth. We’re grateful for Carlyle’s continued partnership and look forward to working with our new strategic partner, KKR.”

+ David Wilson and Atika Lynch, both former Directors of Artist Development at Sony Music’s AWAL, have announced the launch of Cltr;shft, a fractional executive firm specializing in digital marketing, content, audience growth, and culture strategy. Wilson joins as Co-Founder and Fractional Head of Content & Culture Strategy, based in Los Angeles, and Lynch as Co-Founder and Fractional Head of Audience Growth & Culture Strategy, based in New York City.

The announcement states, “Through an approach the founders call culture architecture, the firm identifies what makes a client culturally meaningful, builds the narrative around it, and develops the content systems and audience-growth strategies that create the conditions for scale. As fractional executives, Wilson and Lynch work with clients on a project, fractional, or advisory basis, providing senior-level leadership without requiring them to build an entire department.” Wilson was previously with Nettwerk Music Group, while Lynch held roles at RCA Records, and Tommy Hilfiger.

n7p0wt.title: ‘Love Island’ Winner Bryce Alakai Is Going All-In on His Music Career
n7p0wt.content:
No one can accuse Bryce Alakai of not being dedicated to craft. The 30-year-old, who broke out as the winner of Love Island alongside his now-girlfriend Trinity Tatum, has been steadily growing his profile as a music producer and DJ in the wake of the show. While it’s common for reality stars to pivot in another field after their breakthrough moment, Alakai has been hustling in the space long before the dating competition series.

When the FAA issued a ground stop on Nov. 13, halting all flights around the country, Alakai found himself in a bit of a pickle. He had four shows back-to-back that weekend. Thankfully, he’d made it from Toronto to Atlanta, but that’s where things got tricky. The flights from Atlanta to Florida were canceled, so instead of canceling the shows, like others might’ve, he got in a car and drove about eight hours to his Florida shows.

Alakai and Tatum were fan favorites, eventually winning the show’s eighth season earlier this year. Tatum remains his biggest cheerleader, and the feeling is mutual. “It’s just cool because we’re doing different lanes. She’s so deep in fashion. She’s enveloped in that world. I’m obviously maxed out in music right now,” he tells The Hollywood Reporter on a Zoom. “We’re supporting each other’s dreams.”

With a new single “Conscience,” released on Nov. 20 through Ultra Records, Alakai is going all-in on his career as a musician. “I wanted my first release with Ultra to be just a very happy song, very upbeat,” he says.

“I like the lyrics because it always reminds me of Trinity — fall in love with your best friend,” he says. “The whole point of [the song] is just got to live your life, make your mistakes, do what you got to do — but also just enjoy the ride.”

Below, Alakai speaks with THR about producing, balancing his relationship with post-Love Island fame and his new single.

Have the last few months been just nonstop for you?

It’s been literally the definition of zero to 100.

Were you anticipating that or hoping for that?

No. I was 29, turning 30. I was in that place in my life, where it’d be nice to have a person. … I always thought if something comes from it outside of that, that’d be great. But I didn’t think it would be to the extent that it is. I thought it’d be pretty minor. Oh, you got a deal here or there and then you move on with your life. This has been crazy. But I have such a good team that just took the little fire and fanned the shit out of it.

Alakai.

Elias Tahan

Are you hearing from people after your sets? Are they excited?

It’s insane to be honest. I was in Toronto for that show [I’d mentioned]. Even the venue told me it was the fastest-selling show they’d ever had there. I was so excited to be there because it was such a big crowd. It was like 2,500 people. They’re all hard tickets. Dude, when I walked out, everyone was just screaming. It was crazy. I get the adrenaline. I probably shouldn’t do this, but I check a lot of what people have said after the show because I’m just curious. I’m always trying to see how people are receiving what we’re doing, and 99 percent is all positive. That makes me feel good. I had a girl send me a message the other night [that] said it was the best night she’s ever had in her life. I was reading it, I was like, “That’s insane.” Obviously those things are pretty validating, but I feel like the overall response has been really positive.

This is obviously something you were doing before Love Island, but have you felt people question if you’re taking it seriously in the wake of the show?

Oh, 100 percent. Thankfully I had all my stuff on TikTok already posted up from the past years, so there’s obviously videos of me DJing. Three weeks before I went to Fiji, I opened for Carlita and John Summit, which was my biggest show to date. I was already getting a little traction with it. We were starting to make some moves. When I got off [of Love Island] I saw that everyone kind of recognized [I’d been doing it], so it created a different … I think that’s why maybe the shows have been doing so well, there was already that layer before. At first, the first show, I think people were questioning if I could do it. “Just because he did it before doesn’t mean he is actually good.” After each one of these shows, the credibility has slowly gone up. Now, we’re releasing this new song on Nov. 20 with Ultra. I just feel like I’ve gotten a lot of industry backing that is pretty rare from something like this. The collab interests that I’ve been getting, and the sessions I’ve been doing have been in — it’s been insane. I always feel like I’m in a dream because I feel like with any other career, you see the progression in front of you. With this, it was literally just zero to full on go mode, which I’m really grateful for. It is surreal just because it’s like you’re just jumping straight in.

There’s not much downtime these days, right? You’re also starting this new life with another person, so that’s an added element as well.

That definitely adds a layer to it. I’ve been with her today. We had just flew back last night, I’m with her today and then I have to fly to Vegas tomorrow. Thankfully, she’s coming to Vegas too a couple days later, but it really makes it so I have to check in with her and balance the time. It’s just hard because with these dates, I want to be my best at these performances, but I also don’t want to neglect her and make her ever feel like she’s not my priority because she is. It’s just a balancing game I’ve been learning that I haven’t had to do before and to make sure I water both aspects of my life equally.

I imagine she’s also quite busy.

Today, I have two sessions after this call and then she has an interview and then another thing and then shooting a video. We come back at night. All this shit just happened. It’s just a balancing thing on both of us, and we’re figuring it out. But with how busy we both are, it definitely doesn’t make it easier. I think our communication is so good that we figure it out.

18023e3.title: Claude rolling out updated Android app with Material 3 Expressive redesign
18023e3.content:
Anthropic is rolling out a new Claude app for Android that picks up a Material 3 Expressive redesign.

Confirmed on Twitter/X by Anthropic Product Manager Robert Bye, Claude is now rolling out a Material 3 Expressive redesign for its Android app that, while not a full embrace of Google’s design language, does make a clear attempt to better fit in on Android.

The updated design picks up a bottom-bar UI as opposed to relying fully on the old hamburger menu – it still exists, but it’s mainly for chat history now. You can see M3 elements throughout the app, including in the model switcher and the background of chats. It’s clearly themed to match Anthropic’s aesthetic, and there’s no obvious implementation of Material You colors, but it all fits within the general Material 3 guidelines – much more so than the original app.

The one flaw we spotted was the predictive back implementation, which gets a neat animation to move the search bar but is supposed to show a preview of the previous screen, but that’s just nit-picking, really.

The new Claude app for Android is rolling out now.

1kowxk7.title: Chuck Lorre, ‘Grey’s Anatomy’ EP Zoanne Clack, ‘A Different World’ Boss Felicia Pride Join Lineup for SIE Society’s Impact+Profit26 (Exclusive)
1kowxk7.content:
The SIE Society (Social Impact Entertainment Society) has unveiled the lineup for Impact+Profit26, its flagship conference “showing that storytellers don’t have to choose between impact and profit.”

TV uber-creator Chuck Lorre, Grey’s Anatomy EP Zoanne Clack and A Different World showrunner Felicia Pride are among those scheduled to take part in the two-day event, which is set for Dec. 7-8.

In addition, entertainment-education pioneer Miguel Sabido has been tapped to receive the SIE Impact Entertainment Visionaries Award at the conference, which will be held for the first time at USC Annenberg, home of the Hollywood, Health & Society, a program of the USC Norman Lear Center.

Organizers said the new venue carries special meaning for the field. USC Annenberg’s connection to impact storytelling traces back to the pioneering Soap Summits of the 1990s and early 2000s, which helped spark television’s social impact movement and paved the way for Hollywood, Health & Society.

More than 250 producers, executives, financiers and changemakers are expected to attend the conference, which is presented for the fourth consecutive year in collaboration with the Johns Hopkins Center for Communication Programs.

“Bringing Impact+Profit to USC Annenberg connects us to the history of entertainment education in Hollywood,” said Will Nix, a founder and co-executive director of the SIE Society, whose creative work as a producer includes film, television, theater and digital media productions. “For four years, Johns Hopkins Center for Communication Programs has helped us bring evidence and storytelling into the same room. Impact+Profit is built on partnerships, and we’re grateful to every collaborator who makes it possible.”

Sabido will be honored on Day 1 of the event. The presentation will take place during “The Man Who Proved Stories Can Change the World: A Conversation With Miguel Sabido,” where Sabido will be joined onstage by Robert Rippberger, a founder and co-executive director of the SIE Society, filmmaker and author of The Power of Storytelling: Social Impact Entertainment.

“Long before anyone had a name for this field, Miguel showed the world that a story told with care and purpose could change how millions of people live their lives,” Rippberger said. “His work is the blueprint for what social impact entertainment can achieve. As we celebrate his legacy, we’re also challenging the next generation of storytellers to carry that vision forward with the same courage and rigor.”

The conference will close with “A Conversation With Chuck Lorre,” featuring the Golden Globe-winning writer and producer behind such comedy hits as The Big Bang Theory, Two and a Half Men, Mom, Young Sheldon and Georgie & Mandy’s First Marriage. Lorre, who also founded the Chuck Lorre Family Foundation, will sit down with Jay Sures, vice chairman of United Talent Agency, for a closing-night discussion on his career and his philanthropic work.

Other highlights on the lineup:

“Still Waiting to Be Seen: Women 50+”: A session featuring the latest research from the Geena Davis Institute, director Rachel Feldman (Lilly, The Rookie, Criminal Minds, Blue Bloods) and showrunner Felicia Pride (A Different World), moderated by the Institute’s CEO Madeline Di Nonno.

“Yes, And… Improv and the Future of Impact Storytelling”: The Groundlings’ Michael Churven and actors Jodie Sweetin (Full House, Fuller House) and Yetide Badaki (American Gods, This Is Us), moderated by Anjuli Kronheim Katz, executive director of the Committee for the First Amendment.

Taboo Topics!: Grey’s Anatomy executive producer Zoanne Clack, Ted writer Chelsea Davison and USC Norman Lear Center Director of Research Operations Adam Rogers, moderated by Kate Folb of Hollywood, Health & Society.

Moving Pictures and Saving Lives: Ann Lee of CORE and Natalie Tran of CAA Community & Impact, moderated by The Hollywood Reporter’s Stacey Wilson Hunt.

Music & Movement: Celena Fields (EVEN), A.D. Johnson (Mass Appeal) and Tony Ferguson (Society House), moderated by Soren Baker, author of The History of Gangster Rap.

NBCUniversal’s The Good Daughter: A featured session on the Peacock limited series, now streaming in full. Based on Karin Slaughter’s bestselling novel and starring Rose Byrne and Meghann Fahy, the six-episode drama follows two sisters who confront their painful past to uncover the truth.

“Beyond the Bars”: Writer-producer Mark Goffman (The Irrational, The Umbrella Academy, Bull, White Collar, The West Wing), Renaldo Hudson of The Death Penalty Project, LOHAS partner Tami Kesselman and Rosebuds Reading Collective CEO Nora Fried on how storytelling shapes perceptions of the justice system.

“Building Your Finance Plan in a Changing Landscape”: Legion M’s Paul Scanlan, Entertainment Partners’ Joe Chianese and others on financing impact projects, presented with conference sponsor First Entertainment Credit Union.

Additional sessions will focus on AI and social media for measuring impact, reality TV as a force for good, faith and media, the podcast-to-feature pipeline, grassroots impact for independent filmmakers, and a hands-on workshop on designing transitional characters with the Sabido Method.

The Hollywood Reporter is a media sponsor of Impact+Profit26. The event is also supported by First Entertainment Credit Union, NBCUniversal, World Bank Group; media sponsor KCRW; and partners Population Media Center and Schulz Entertainment Law and the UTA Foundation.

Regular tickets are $375 and student tickets are $150 (valid enrollment required). Tickets include two days of panels and workshops, six networking sessions, and food and drink. Registered attendees can use the SIE Society conference app for the agenda, curated networking and badge scanning. Tickets and the full agenda can be found at conference.siesociety.org

The SIE Society is a global community of nearly 1,800 entertainment, corporateand nonprofit professionals, from all storytelling media platforms, who are working at the intersection of storytelling and social change. The SIE Society works to support collaboration and measurable impact across industries through curated programming, thought leadership and year-round engagement.

szizun.title: Xbox Helix могла стать консолью мечты, но Microsoft рискует всё испортить
szizun.content:
Опрос

3DNews Новости Software игры Xbox Helix могла стать консолью мечты, н...

реклама

Новости Software

Самое интересное в обзорах

24.11.2026 [01:17],

Xbox Helix изначально задумывался как проект с бесплатным многопользовательским онлайн-режимом, полноценными играми для ПК и платформой Steam, однако смена руководства игрового подразделения, рост стоимости комплектующих и пересмотр стратегии компании поставили эти намерения под вопрос.
Источник изображения: Microsoft

По данным Windows Central, первоначальный план строился на том, что Xbox Helix сможет запускать не только игры для консолей Xbox, но и игры для ПК, в том числе из сторонних магазинов и, в частности, из Steam. В этом случае пользователи получили бы доступ к более широкой библиотеке игр, не ограничиваясь собственной экосистемой Xbox. По своей концепции такая система напоминает портативную консоль Xbox Ally, только в формате домашнего устройства (без встроенного экрана и кнопок на корпусе).
Отказ от обязательной подписки для многопользовательского онлайн-режима был частью этого замысла. Поскольку Helix должна была поддерживать обычные компьютерные игры и сервисы, Microsoft пришлось бы разрешить пользователям играть по сети без дополнительной платы. Однако при таком подходе компания лишилась бы регулярных финансовых поступлений от подписок, которые сейчас помогают компенсировать расходы на выпуск консолей и содержание игровых студий. При этом стоимость самой Helix пришлось бы рассчитывать так, чтобы окупить производство за счёт продажи устройства.

Первоначальный план разрабатывали при прежнем руководстве Xbox — Филе Спенсере (Phil Spencer) и Саре Бонд (Sarah Bond), после ухода которых игровое подразделение возглавила Аша Шарма (Asha Sharma). Затем публичные заявления представителей Xbox стали указывать на более сдержанный подход: Helix по-прежнему должна запускать компьютерные игры, но основой устройства может стать привычная консольная оболочка, а не полноценная среда Windows с доступом к сторонним магазинам.
На планы Microsoft влияет и ситуация с комплектующими. Рост цен на оперативную память и другие компоненты делает производство нового игрового устройства дороже. Кроме того, открытый доступ к Steam может помешать компании возвращать пользователей в собственную экосистему Xbox. Тем более, что внутренний анализ Microsoft показал, что владельцы портативной Xbox Ally часто выбирают Steam, когда получают такую возможность. Поэтому не исключено, что под запуском компьютерных игр на Helix в итоге будет подразумеваться поддержка версий для ПК из экосистемы Xbox, а не полноценный доступ к магазину Valve.
Отмена платы за сетевую игру также лишила бы Microsoft одного из источников регулярного дохода. По оценке Windows Central, подписки Xbox Game Pass Core могут приносить сотни миллионов долларов в год, а возможно, и больше. При этом текущие Xbox Series X и Series S, как отмечает издание, уже продаются с убытком для компании.

В качестве одного из вариантов Microsoft может отменить плату за доступ к многопользовательскому режиму только на Helix, но оставить обязательную подписку для владельцев предыдущих консолей Xbox, или выпустить несколько версий устройства с разными возможностями. Впрочем, окончательный вариант Helix пока неизвестен. Для условно-бесплатных игр, таких как Fortnite, Overwatch и Roblox подписка Xbox и сейчас не требуется, поэтому речь идёт прежде всего о доступе к сетевым режимам платных игр.

17o8syp.title: Tom Cullen,Joe Locke's ‘Black Church Bay’ Sells to North America
17o8syp.content:
Rhys Marc Jones’s “Black Church Bay,” a mystery thriller starring “Heartstopper” breakout Joe Locke and Tom Cullen (“Weekend”), has been bought by Strand Releasing for North America.

Jones’ feature debut, “Black Church Bay” follows a man whose world unravels after a secret relationship ends in tragedy. Set against the backdrop of Anglesey in North Wales, the thriller explores gay repression, identity and the lengths people will go to conceal their true selves.

The deal was negotiated by Strand Releasing’s Jon Gerrans and The Bureau Sales’ Clémentine Hugot. Strand is planning a summer 2027 theatrical release.

“We’re thrilled to be working with The Bureau Sales on this innovative thriller that confronts complicated issues of gay repression and Cullen and Locke’s performances are so beautifully directed by Jones and create a real suspenseful thriller that is satisfying,” said Marcus Hu, co-president of Strand Releasing.

“Black Church Bay” world premiered at Zurich and went to play at Busan and the BFI London Film Festival.

“The film is the culmination of my thematic obsessions – a mystery thriller exploring notions of acceptance, authenticity and repression; how it is often our contradictions that define who we are and what we become,” said Jones.

“Black Church Bay” was shot last year on location in Anglesey and produced by Alex Polunin of Scotland-based Ossian International and Tristan Goligher of London-based The Bureau.

Polunin, who previously produced Jones’ short films “Pale Saint” and “Father of the Bride,” developed the film from its inception.

“One of the things that’s most distinctive and unique about this idea is the way in which it combines Rhys’s thematic and formal interests as a filmmaker – specifically in exploring the queer experience in such a nuanced way, but also through the genre engine of a thriller,” Polunin said.

Goligher, meanwhile, pointed to Jones’ ability to build and sustain suspense while exploring morally complex characters.

“It’s really rare to see short films where a filmmaker can create – and sustain – tension in the way that he did. This script does the same thing,“ Goligher said. “We’ve had a lot of very positive messaging around the gay experience in recent years but it’s also not everyone’s experience. Rhys wrote a very specific story about a very specific person and their experience, and I have no doubt that chimes with many people in the UK and the world.”

“But watching someone deal with a moral dilemma – trying to wrestle with the question of should they, and can they, do the right thing at their own cost – that’s also a very universal dilemma,“ added Goligher.

The film was developed with BBC Film, iFeatures and the Cannes Film Festival’s Cinéfondation Résidence. Financing came from BBC Film, Ffilm Cymru Wales, Screen Scotland and private backers including Los Angeles-based Manzini Films, U.K.-based Elephant Film and 1C6 Films, Kamila Serkebaeva and Brazil-based Daniel Staut.

Strand Releasing’s current slate includes Gregg Araki’s 4K restoration of “Mysterious Skin” and David Pablos’ “On the Road,” which represents Mexico in the Oscar race.

18bl3dh.title: Anthropic launches Claude Ship, letting AI agents review, fix, and approve code changes
18bl3dh.content:
Anthropic is moving from having Claude write code to helping developers decide when that code is ready to ship. On Monday, the newly public AI company announced the launch of Claude Ship, a suite of AI agents for automating code reviews, fixes, and approvals of routine code changes.

The latter is the more interesting part of this new set of tools, as AI coding tools already offered code review features before now. What’s notable about Claude Ship is not just that it can review proposed code changes and identify and address problems, but that it also includes an agent that can approve code changes automatically based on policies set by a development team.

Image Credits:Anthropic

The launch arrives at a time when AI coding agents have become increasingly capable of generating substantial amounts of code, leading to bottlenecks in reviewing and approving the code changes before they go live. With Claude Ship, the idea is to automate even more of the work involved in the development process, essentially by delegating approval authority to an AI agent itself.

“Most teams want a person to approve every change, and that’s easy to keep up with when people write every line. But a lot of developers build with agents now,” a company blog post explains. “On the Claude Code team, Claude writes most of our code, and we wanted everything after the PR to move that fast too.”

Claude Ship is launching in beta, allowing early adopters to use it to review pull requests (PRs), and then decide what’s ready to merge.

The new offering consists of Code Review, which is already generally available, and two new agents now in beta: PR Steward and Claude Approvals. PR Steward focuses on addressing issues such as failing CI checks, merge conflicts, and feedback from Code Review. It also comments after every push on what it changed and how to roll it back, if needed.

Image Credits:Anthropic

Claude Approvals then applies an approval policy that the team writes as a file in the repository. This approval process can incorporate various signals, including Code Review findings or the company’s own classifiers, with policies written in natural language.

Because the offering is still in beta, Anthropic suggests running the approval functionality in observe-only mode first. Teams can also choose to start with just one repository and set monthly spending limits to have more control over the process.

Anthropic says teams will also still remain in control of where Claude Ship runs, which review settings to use (e.g., Quick, Standard, or Deep), and which changes should be escalated to a human for a decision.

Claude Ship is rolling out to Claude Team and Enterprise plans for repositories on GitHub. Code Review is generally available, while PR Steward and Claude Approvals are in beta.

1amb5d0.title: Skydance Buyouts Impact CBS Stations; Local Chicago Anchor Among Those Departing
1amb5d0.content:
The buyouts across Skydance have impacted CBS’ station group, with a number of staffers taking the package, including a main anchor at the network’s Chicago outlet.

Joe Donlon, co-anchor of CBS 2 Chicago’s 5, 6 and 10 p.m. newscast, is among those leaving, according to sources familiar with the plans. Donlon previously was a lead anchor at WGN-TV from 2018 to 2020 and helped launch Nexstar’s NewsNation. He previously was anchor in Portland for 21 years.

Other on-air figures also have confirmed their exits. They include CBS4 Denver investigative reporter Brian Maass, who wrote on X that he would be departing on Dec. 4 after 43 years at CBS.

“The offer and the timing just seem right,” Maass wrote, confirming a report in Inside the News Colorado newsletter.

“It’s a moment filled with gratitude, pride and sadness. I’ve loved this work, believed deeply in its purpose, and never lost my appreciation for the importance of journalism.”

In Pittsburgh, at CBS’ station there, anchor Ken Rice and investigative reporter Andy Sheehan took the buyout, according to news site TribLive.com.

CBS has not said how many staffers took the offer.

A CBS Stations spokesperson said, “As previously reported, voluntary buyout offers were made available to eligible employees across the company. We recognize the interest in learning which anchors and reporters may be leaving our local stations. These are deeply personal decisions, and we want to approach each departure with the respect, care and gratitude our colleagues deserve.

The spokesperson added, “We are tremendously grateful for the contributions these individuals have made to our stations and the communities they serve. We also recognize the meaningful relationships our anchors and reporters have built with viewers who welcome them into their homes every day. We believe these departures are best acknowledged thoughtfully within the newsroom first and at the appropriate time.”

At CBS News, those taking the buyouts included staffers in the London bureau, as well as other areas across the news division and on 60 Minutes. Less than 10% of those offered the buyouts accepted them, according to a source familiar with the plans.

Skydance is looking to trim $6 billion in costs across the company in the aftermath of its acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery. The merger has put CBS News and CNN under the same corporate owner.

gh-1439659530.title: GitHub - berobloom/redcat-rrr-re: Reverse engineering of RedCat's Razende Rekenrace (1996, DOS) and a from-scratch C port for Linux and the browser (WebAssembly). Needs your own copy of the game data.
gh-1439659530.content:
A study of the 1996 DOS game RedCat's Razende Rekenrace (Davilex), a
racing game for primary-school arithmetic, and a reimplementation in C that
plays it on Linux and in the browser.

The research half is notes on how the original works, worked out from its
executables (Watcom C, DOS/4GW) and its data, and from experiments with it
running under DOSBox-X. Each finding records the code addresses it rests on
and how sure it is.
The port is a new engine in C (SDL2) that reads the original game data
unchanged. It plays the game's round as the original does: the intro film,
the menu, the races, the four kinds of arithmetic exercises in between, the
podium and the high scores. The same sources build for the web with
Emscripten.

All of these are the port, captured in the first world, De Welkomstrace.
The game itself is not included. You need your own copy of the CD.
Nothing here changes or redistributes the original files.
Matching decompilation

Next to the port, the original's C is being rebuilt function by function so
that it compiles to the same bytes, with the game's own compiler: Watcom
C/C++ 10.5, wcc386 -3r -s -ox, under Wine. It starts with RRR.EXE, the
race. docs/RRRPROGRESS.HTML lists every function:
search it, filter it by status or subsystem, and click a near miss to see its
instruction diff against the game. PROGRESS.md has the same
numbers as tables. reverse-engineering/tools/progress.py writes all three
from a fresh build. The workflow is in MATCHING.md, the
compiler set-up in
reverse-engineering/watcom.md.
src/check.sh # compile src/*.c (one object per module), compare every function
.work/venv/bin/python reverse-engineering/tools/progress.py # rewrite PROGRESS.md and docs/RRRPROGRESS.*
Playing
You need CMake, a C compiler and SDL2. Point the launcher at the game's data:
the CD root, or the installed C:\DAVILEX\RCREKEN (the directory with
RCS.IND, RC.IND and TRANS.DAT):
port/play.sh <game data dir> # the whole game, intro first
port/play.sh <game data dir> --no-intro # straight to the menu
port/play.sh <game data dir> --race # straight into a race
It builds the port the first time. The game directory is only read: the
record (RRRIO.INF), the pupils' results and the high scores go to
~/.local/share/Davilex/RedCat, or to the directory given with --save.
The other options are in port/README.md.
In the browser
port/web/build.sh # needs Emscripten (emcc)
port/web/serve.sh # then open http://localhost:8080/redcat.html
The page asks for your game folder (the CD or the installed game) once and
keeps the files it needs in the browser's storage.
Layout

Path
Contents

research/discoveries.md
What has been established, with evidence

research/hypotheses.md
Ideas that are not settled yet

research/open-questions.md
Open and resolved questions

reverse-engineering/
Reference docs: executables, file formats, architecture, running the original under DOSBox-X

reverse-engineering/tools/
LE loader, disassembler, function finder, xrefs, Unicorn emulation and the DOSBox-X driver; wc/: the Watcom compile-and-compare tools

reverse-engineering/analysis/
Function lists, names, CD inventory

src/
The matching decompilation: rrr.h, one .c per known module (new2io.c, order.c), rrr.c for the rest, check.sh, the baseline and the near-miss list (MATCHING.md)

port/
The C port; port/README.md is its detailed manual

port/web/
The WebAssembly build

port/rctools/
Python tools for the game's archives, images and maps

How the research works
Each finding carries a label: CONFIRMED, STRONGLY SUPPORTED, LIKELY or
SPECULATIVE. The notes never present an inference as fact. Evidence from the
binaries and from runtime experiments comes before outside documentation.
Where the port's behaviour comes from the original, its source comments name
the address it was taken from, for example 0x1103e for the start lights.
Where the port deliberately differs, port/README.md says so. The working
rules, and how to set up .work/, are in AGENTS.md.
The 32-bit programs are LE executables, which most tools do not open.
reverse-engineering/tools/leparse.py applies their fixups and writes each
as an ELF image at its run-time addresses. The original runs in a patched
DOSBox-X that reverse-engineering/tools/dosrun.py drives on a hidden
display: keys, screenshots, memory and save states; see
reverse-engineering/runtime-dosbox.md.
The tools need Python 3 with capstone, and some unicorn.
Status
The game's round is playable from the intro to the high scores. Not ported
yet: the winner's film after a world's last race (the podium stands in), the
closing film, the menu's joystick set-up and the mouse pointer in the
exercises. The unanswered questions are in research/open-questions.md.

Foundation, either version 3 of the License, or (at your option) any later

It covers this project's own code and notes, not the game.

1mysmf8.title: Supertake raises $20M to let AI agents turn your market predictions into stock portfolios
1mysmf8.content:
AI investing startup Supertake has an interesting premise: What if your “takes” on the market could make you money without you having to pick stocks yourself? The service lets people turn their ideas into real investment portfolios, using frontier AI models and trading agents.

Now, the company has raised $20 million in seed funding to grow its business. The round was led by venture firm Adjacent (Nico Wittenborn), with participation from Coinbase Ventures and Union Square Ventures (USV). Numerous angel investors also joined, including Nat Friedman, who’s currently head of product at Meta Superintelligence Labs; Vercel CEO Guillermo Rauch; renowned product manager Nikita Bier; investor Scott Belsky; and Nemil Dalal, a former Coinbase exec who is now a visiting partner at Y Combinator.

Michael Mignano originally incubated the startup at USV. He is the co-founder and former CEO of the podcasting platform Anchor, which Spotify acquired in 2019 for over $150 million. After leading Spotify’s podcasting business as “Head of Talk” for a few years, he joined the team at Lightspeed as a venture partner, betting on AI companies like Suno and Granola. He also co-founded Oboe, an AI education startup, and joined USV as a general partner in April.

Image Credits:Supertake

“We really believed there was an opportunity to make investing more democratized…and give everyone and anyone the ability to invest in their own insights and beliefs and ideas,” Mignano said. While he will continue in his role as founder and executive chairman, he’s now brought in a team to run the company day to day.

The team includes co-founders Lincoln Murr (CEO) and John Peterson (CTO). Both joined from Coinbase, where, Mignano notes, they were the heads of AI product and engineering, leading launches like Coinbase advisor, Coinbase for agents, agentic wallets, and others.

The startup arrives as AI continues to make inroads into financial services, but allowing AI to take over people’s actual investments requires a new level of trust. Supertake is betting that people will ultimately be willing to take that leap, given recent improvements in frontier AI models.

Currently, Supertake works with Coinbase and Robinhood, and the company intends to expand to more brokerages over time. The idea is that you can explain, in broad, natural language, what you believe about how the world is going to change, and Supertake’s AI will iterate with you back and forth to turn that idea into a “take” that’s investable.

Under the hood, the startup is leveraging frontier AI technology and tools, combined with its own proprietary software that directs and limits what the AI can do.

Image Credits:Supertake

Supertake’s users’ ideas are tracked on a leaderboard on the site, so others who agree can invest alongside them. For instance, there’s currently an idea on the leaderboard about looksmaxxing and longevity becoming more of a trend, where the portfolio includes certain pharma and cosmetic companies that could potentially benefit.

For now, these portfolios consist of stock picks, but the team wants to expand the service over time to handle other types of transactions, like shorts, derivatives, perpetuals, long exposure, or even prediction markets — the latter handled through partnerships with companies in that space.

Despite these “takes” seeming like bets on what could happen next in a given market, Murr stresses that this doesn’t make Supertake itself a prediction market.

Image Credits:Supertake example (screenshot)

“We think it’s a novel and very much improved way to create what was previously considered the robo-advisor experience,” he says. “When that came out, it had this amazing vision and direction of allowing people to have digital asset management. We think now is actually the time for that, with AI agents being so widely proliferated.”

“I don’t think this is necessarily a prediction market by any means. The idea of natural language translation into an underlying set of assets feels different in that regard,” he says.

Still, the startup could wade into short-term predictions if a user’s take involves something they believe could happen in the near future, like who might win an election.

“We’re primarily focused on the longer, medium-term holdings today. But that being said, we don’t want to preclude people from building out very hyper short-term strategies that might exist,” Murr adds.

Image Credits:Screenshot

To address people’s concerns over AI managing their money, Supertake’s team says it’s implementing certain guardrails and spend limits. For instance, the AI has no ability to deposit or withdraw funds on a user’s behalf without their explicit consent. There are also drift limits in place so the portfolio stays balanced, plus allow and deny lists (meaning which assets the AI may and may not trade), real-time monitoring for anomalous activity, tools to set trade size limits, and a restriction that keeps agents from seeing the user’s brokerage credentials.

“We view it as somewhat analogous to self-driving cars, actually, where there is a spectrum here of both trust and technological innovations that are happening,” says Murr. “Where a few years ago you may not feel comfortable getting in a car that has lane assist, but today you get in a Waymo, and it’s like nothing. And we think that there’s a very similar progression happening with the agentic finance space, and we’re far further along in the technological spectrum than people think.”

Access to Supertake is still behind a waitlist while in beta, but the founders said they’ve put their money where their mouths are. Murr and Peterson are letting it manage “tens of thousands” and “thousands” of dollars, respectively.

Mignano, meanwhile, says he has Supertake managing “hundreds of thousands” of dollars.

With the new funding, which follows a $2 million pre-seed round, Supertake aims to expand its team in areas like engineering, design, growth marketing, and others. Mignano and Murr are in New York, while Peterson is in the Austin area but commutes to New York at times. The team says it hopes to figure out a hybrid work model as it grows.

wxfil6.title: Elon Musk and others rejoice as Jensen Huang is reinstated at Nvidia amid scandal
wxfil6.content:
A handful of tech CEOs, including Elon Musk, are celebrating Jensen Huang’s return to Nvidia. Despite being caught in three affairs — including one with an alleged Chinese spy that has triggered multiple congressional investigations over national security concerns — Huang was reinstated as CEO and president of Nvidia on Monday morning.

“The mistake has been corrected,” Tesla and SpaceX leader Elon Musk wrote on X about Huang’s return.

Musk had been among the most vocal tech leaders to advocate for Huang.

“I think it’s like kicking Michael Jordan off your team when you’re on a winning streak, and it just doesn’t seem like a good thing for shareholders,” Musk said last week at the DealBook Summit.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman had taken a more neutral stance, commenting last week, “It’s hard to imagine the AI industry without Jensen.”

Altman had experienced a similar situation when he was ousted as CEO of OpenAI, then reinstated days later. After the announcement that Huang would return, Altman simply posted, “Jensen!” Many other tech CEOs have similarly refrained from commenting on the matter, given the shifting politics surrounding Huang’s ouster and reinstatement, as well as the national security concerns at the center of the controversy.

In addition to Musk, Binance co-founder and former CEO Changpeng Zhao (CZ), who served prison time for failing to stop criminal activity on the Binance crypto exchange, is also supportive of Huang.

“Glad to see @JensenHuang back,” CZ posted on X with a clapping hands emoji.

Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, who had been among 200,000 signatories on an open letter calling for Huang’s reinstatement, wrote on X, “Jensen’s return will be a demonstration of American resiliency to corporate, political and journalistic missteps.”

Another signatory on the open letter, former Uber CEO Travis Kalanick, who had similarly been driven out of the company he founded after scandals, also voiced his support for Huang on X.

When Nvidia’s stock tanked in reaction to Huang’s ousting, billionaire hedge fund manager Bill Ackman said he believes that the Nvidia board was “not acting in the best interest of shareholders nor in a manner consistent with their fiduciary duties.” As Nvidia’s stock began to rebound Monday morning, Ackman wrote, “The wisdom of the crowd prevails.”

The attitude toward Huang’s return is not as celebratory outside of the tech industry. Across the political spectrum, some elected officials are skeptical about President Donald Trump’s claims that Huang’s return does not threaten national security.

“No national security risk? Based on what?” wrote Senator John Cornyn (R-TX).

Jensen Huang had multiple affairs including with subordinates and an alleged Chinese spy. His own board described his behavior as lacking “candor.” I’ve served on a public company board. His behavior does not support reinstatement.Nvidia’s decision today doesn’t excuse Jensen…— Senator Pete Ricketts (@SenatorRicketts) November 23, 2026

Senator Pete Ricketts (R-NB) added, “Nvidia’s decision today doesn’t excuse Jensen Huang from testifying before Congress. It also doesn’t absolve Nvidia of answering for national security concerns and unaccounted-for chips. I look forward to Mr. Huang coming to the Senate in December.”

Huang is still expected to testify publicly before the Senate Banking Committee on December 3, as well as privately before three House committees.

jpv9b5.title: BYD Barred from Selling Ti7 SUV in EU Because of a Copycat Design
jpv9b5.content: A Dutch court has barred BYD from selling its Ti7 mid-size SUV in the European Union over a case of copyright infringement, an Automotive News report shows. It’s easy to spot why, given that BYD’s Ti7’s looks are strikingly similar to the boxy shape of the Land Rover Defender.BYD said it strongly disagrees with the ruling and plans to appeal the ruling in court.A Dutch court has ruled that BYD cannot sell the Ti7 mid-size three-row SUV in the European Union, according to a report from Automotive News. According to the report, a preliminary ruling from the Dutch court found BYD guilty of copyright infringement, with the Ti7 ruled to be a dupe of the Land Rover Defender.Jaguar Land Rover (JLR) brought the case against BYD earlier this year after the Chinese automaker announced that it would launch the car in the United Kingdom in 2027. The preliminary ruling marks a significant setback in BYD’s recent explosive expansion into Europe.BYDMichael Simari|Car and Driver“In these summary proceedings, the preliminary relief judge rules that the Ti7 infringes the EU design of Jaguar Land Rover,” the court said in its November 20 ruling, AN reported. “The characteristic and distinctive elements of the design are reflected in the BYD Ti7.”The Defender is JLR’s best-selling vehicle globally, with the automaker shipping more than 100,000 units last year. Both vehicles have boxy designs with flat rooflights, squared wheel arches, and, notably, body-colored panels in place of the rear side windows.Unfortunately for JLR, the judge also ruled that the court does not have authority over BYD’s U.K. arm. To that end, JLR is reportedly planning to bring the same claim to the courts in England.According to AN, BYD “strongly disagrees” with the ruling and has plans to appeal the result. “The BYD Ti7 is the result of BYD’s own independent design work and infringes none of JLR’s rights,” the company said. “We will pursue every legal avenue to demonstrate that this decision is incorrect.”While the final ruling will likely take some time before it is announced, the Dutch court has prohibited BYD from producing the Ti7 at its new factory in Hungary, where it was due to begin mass production early next year.➡️ Skip the lot. 1c1lpmx.title: Even Sienna Miller Was Surprised by That ‘War’ Ending
1c1lpmx.content:
Logo text

[This story contains MAJOR spoilers from the War finale.]

Sienna Miller doesn’t quite know why she keeps getting tapped to play women caught up in the public eye. Since breaking out two decades ago as Edie Sedgwick in Factory Girl, the American-born English actress has made a speciality out of portraying women navigating intense media scrutiny — from Alfred Hitchcock’s tormented muse Tippi Hedren in The Girl to the embattled political wives of Showtime’s The Loudest Voice and Netflix’s Anatomy of a Scandal.

“I think it’s less that I’m seeking out these roles and more that those are the roles that people see me as, probably because a famous actress is part of my identity in a way [but] I don’t feel is part of me,” Miller tells The Hollywood Reporter on a recent video call from her home in the U.K. “I feel like an actor who’s not very famous — and a mom. But it’s quite funny to perhaps send myself up by playing heightened versions of whatever I imagine people might assume that to be.”

Miller’s latest TV role is no exception. In creator George Kay’s HBO/Sky legal anthology drama War, which just aired its finale on Thursday in the U.S., Miller plays film star Clara Duval, whose messy, high-profile divorce from Dominic West’s billionaire tech founder Morgan Henderson becomes a feeding frenzy for both the press and their ruthless legal teams. At the center of the dispute is an equitable split of Zephyr — the ostensibly “less toxic” social media platform that Morgan built after watching Carla endure relentless online bullying and that Carla named after Mary Darby Robinson’s poem “Ode to the Muse.”

Though their lawyers push them toward scorched-earth tactics to win at all costs, the pair ultimately choose to settle on their own terms, resulting in a surprisingly optimistic portrait of life after separation. “I think the normalizing of divorce is something that should be more commonplace in the world. It doesn’t have to be hell,” Miller says. “I thought that the ending was very poignant and sweet.”

In the wide-ranging chat below, Miller opens up to THR about shedding her own people-pleasing tendencies to play a “narcissistic” (but surprisingly sympathetic) actress, why she thinks Carla really came out on top in the divorce — and how she reflects now on her own experience of being tabloid fodder in her 20s: “I’m more in a kind of anthropological way interested in it [now], because I feel maybe from some PTSD that I am separate from it.”

***

War creator George Kay has said he wanted an actual movie star to play Carla, but he very intentionally did not want to let any of your own personal experiences influence the writing of the character. In hindsight, what did you find most appealing about embodying someone in an esoteric world that you already know so intimately yourself?

I signed on before I knew what it was, because I only read the pilot, so I was learning on the job very much with this. This isn’t a limited series, but for me, it was. [Writer’s note: Kay confirmed to THR that each season of War will center on a new legal dispute, with the parties being represented by the same group of lawyers at rival London firms Cathcarts & Sons and Taylor & Byrne.]

Sometimes when you do a limited series, you have all eight episodes and you can kind of map something out. But with this, I wouldn’t find out till a few days before we’d start shooting the next block [when] we’d get scripts. So it wasn’t that I made a choice to play somebody in those circumstances, and I don’t know now that I need to do it again. But while I was in it and learning who she was as we were going along, I thought it was interesting to feel like somebody very different in those somewhat familiar circumstances. But I think Carla’s much more steely and less naive than I am.

I wouldn’t want to describe Carla as a narcissist, but she certainly comes across as a little high-strung and self-centered.

No, she’s a narcissist. (Laughs.)

Where do you think her narcissistic nature comes from? Did you establish any kind of backstory that could shed light on what makes her tick?

I think she’s an insecure woman who has had to deal with underestimation, and I don’t think there was one inciting incident. I think you are either one of two personality types — you either have more of a narcissistic personality, or you’re more of an empathetic person. I, as myself, would walk into a room and be concerned or pretty much aware of everybody within that room, and roughly have a temperature gauge on all of them. With Carla, I think she has decided that she’s the most important person in that room, and she doesn’t feel the need to check in with others. I think she channeled whatever abandonment she experienced into that way of being as a defense mechanism, versus my equivalent — which is exhausting, but is also a defense mechanism.

[Playing] that was really fun. Once I made that decision to be like, “She’s not concerned with other people’s feelings or energies, and she’s very much orbiting herself” — it was so uncomfortable at first to be that way. And then anytime I stumbled upon something that my instinct would be to correct, I was like, “No, she wouldn’t bother her.” And then it was quite a liberating choice.

George has also talked about how you brought an unexpected softness to Carla that was not always part of his original conception of the character. Were there any particular moments in the season that you wanted to soften her a little bit or make her more likeable? Did you ever push back on some of her actions or decisions?

I didn’t feel like I needed to make her more likable. I sometimes needed reasons for the decisions about how she was [acting]. I felt like I really pushed back against the kind of hysterical breakdown on the talk show [in episode five], although people really enjoyed that, because I just didn’t want it to fall into any kind of “hysterical woman” trope situation. I didn’t want Morgan to appear reasonable and Carla to appear unhinged, but that’s often the way the world sees these relationships and sees the dynamics between a couple. If she’s ambitious or if she’s ruthless, she’s a bitch; if he is [those same things], he’s a great businessman. I think it does kick up some of those tropes, which I was really trying to push back on until I realized, “Well, maybe it’s a great mirror to see how women are treated and judged.” Obviously, it gets rectified, and she wins that particular battle.

But there were moments in this that I was trying to advocate for her to be more vulnerable, or more soft, or just more three-dimensional. But then if I didn’t find it, I would just lean into her being really unashamedly a bitch or whatever she is. The moment where she couldn’t remember her son’s age — I was like, “That’s a huge thing [to forget]!” And we were learning this as we were going on. I’m like, “Does she not know her son’s age?” And then I would talk to other cast [members] who were like, “Actually, it’s kind of funny. Just do it.” But I was trying to fight for her a bit in moments.

Dominic West and Sienna Miller in the end of War.

HBO

Even though you and Dominic play the leads of this season, your characters don’t actually spend a lot of time together because they’re always busy strategizing with their own lawyers. What did all of the brief glimpses of Carla and Morgan — in the back of a limousine, in an elevator, in the back alley of the courthouse waiting for their cars in the rain — reveal to you about the nature of their relationship?

I think the thing that Carla and Morgan were missing was time together, and time and energy spent on each other. When they’re forced into those situations, other than the car at the very beginning, I think they realized that there was so much there that was probably salvageable or that they cared about. And once you get into a war situation and it’s you versus them, it’s very easy to forget those moments, the good things. But I think what probably comes across in those poignant moments is a sense of love buried underneath all of it, or consideration at least, or some form of emotion, which I think the lawyers are very good at hiding from you.

Carla’s relationship with Morgan is also very much shaped by their own financial circumstances — he is now a billionaire tech founder, and she has been experiencing a lull in her acting career and a significant dip in her income.

I think through the process of divorce and how acrimonious that is and how savage it is, you can either really sink into the resentment and the loathing, or you can remember what it was that brought you together. In the cross-examination [during the last two episodes], we’re talking about moments when we first met. Parts of it are quite therapeutic for them.

I think she genuinely feels entitled to something for Zephyr. I think she really does feel like she contributed more than he is allowing to be let on to the formation of that company, but she’s just vengeful. I don’t even know that it was ever about the money. I think she was just unhappy and he was unhappy, and then it got ugly. She kind of made it ugly, but that’s because she was convinced he cheated. It’s a whole mess, but there are threads within it that I also struggle to follow. So I put it down to just them being erratic and love not being a linear thing.

Carla and Morgan clearly could have settled their divorce at any point during mediation or arbitration, but it’s not until the end of their two-day trial that they decide to reach a fair settlement on their own terms without any outside intervention. In their last scene together, the two of them share a lovely moment on the beach in Normandy, and they are last seen walking back to her cottage to have a hot chocolate with Gabe (Aran Murphy, son of Cilian), Carla’s son from a previous relationship. What did you make of the resolution of their relationship?

I think they’re both battle-weary by that point, and they’ve seen all of the duplicity amongst the legal teams, and that side of things is so ugly. They’ve humiliated each other publicly and been backed into corners, and I think they don’t recognize themselves in some of those moments. I found I was expecting more fireworks at the ending. (Laughs.) And then in reflection, I think the normalizing of divorce is something that should be more commonplace in the world. It doesn’t have to be hell. I thought that the ending was very poignant and sweet.

Basically, what happened was that Dom and I never really got to work together. So anytime we did, we were very happy, which I think serves the story and adds a little sort of something to the scenes. But I found that scene on the beach touching to shoot and surprisingly emotional. But again, there are so many different ways that this could have gone, and I have to defer to the writing team to come up with the best one. I think Carla should have won! I probably was drawn to it becoming more ugly. But actually, the lawyers are the ugly people, and that’s the moral of the story. Even though Carla and Morgan are also ugly and narcissistic. (Laughs.)

What do you think it says about us as a culture that we immediately think of the worst possible scenario for a high-profile divorce?

Well, I don’t know. I think it’s wealthy people. We want to see them being treated like normal people, being dragged through the mud. It’s the same with Succession. We loved watching those people get it wrong and fall apart. I think there must be some kind of schadenfreude. It’s wonderful to be in those aspirational worlds and then wonderful to be reminded that, irrespective of how aspirational this world is or how great it looks from the outside, they’re two people dealing with shit. It’s just with many more zeros on the end of it.

George has told me his theory about what happens to Carla and Morgan’s relationship, but what do you imagine Carla and Morgan’s lives — either together or apart — will look like going forward?

I think they’ll be really good friends, but I think he will regret [the divorce] more than she will. So that’s me defending my character, and Dom would say the same thing about his. (Laughs.)

West and Miller in War.

HBO

Over the last couple of decades, you have played a lot of women — and particularly actresses — who are navigating intense public scrutiny. It’s hard not to think about how the early years of your career in the mid-2000s were overshadowed by British tabloid culture and paparazzi obsession. How do you reflect now on the harsh treatment that you endured in your 20s?

Yeah, it feels so alien to the world that we live in now that it’s almost comical. It’s not comical, but I’m baffled that that existed. The ’90s [had] a lad culture in England, and God forbid, you couldn’t take the piss out of yourself and laugh at yourself. If you couldn’t laugh at yourself or send yourself up, you weren’t worth talking to in England. So I think I kind of absorbed that lad culture and was quite gobby and probably quite fun for them fodder-wise. But the lad culture meant that the paparazzi were just ravenous and unstoppable and aggressive and violent, and it’s just so different to the world [now]. It just would not be allowed; it wouldn’t be tolerated. People on the street wouldn’t stand for it if they saw what was happening.

It was young women that were targeted and cameras up your skirts — just shocking. But you look back and you’re like, “God, that’s not long ago,” and it was absolutely accepted and paid for and devoured. So I’m more in a kind of anthropological way interested in it [now], because I feel maybe from some PTSD that I am separate from it. I can look back on it with curiosity and philosophy versus trauma and just be like, “God, that’s crazy that it wasn’t that long ago, and that’s how we lived.” But pre-social media, in 2008, the whole world shifted. In 2012, it really shifted, but it’s just interesting to look back on that time and to have been such a part of it and feel like it’s so foreign. I think it was too much for anyone to really live like 15 people outside your house and chasing you everywhere you went. I’ve always been the same — I’m quite a normal, grounded person that it just didn’t suit [my life]. I don’t want bodyguards and putting on makeup every day.

You’ve spoken about wanting to take yourself more seriously as an actress, and reaching a point in your life where you are decidedly less interested in hearing other people’s opinions. When did that shift start for you?

I think I always took my work really seriously. I just think it was a battle to be seen as a serious actor in my 20s, but we are way beyond that now. I think when I had my first daughter, life just suddenly felt more serious, and the choices that I was making, they had to be worthy of being away from home and taking my kid on the road, and there was just more levity to each decision. So I feel like the work is something I’ve always taken very seriously, but people didn’t see me as a serious actor until quite a while ago now.

Do you ever worry that playing women who are consistently judged by their image reinforces the narrative you’ve been trying to move past?

It’s interesting. I don’t ever think about that in relation to these actresses. I see them as they should be seen: as people. But I think what I was objecting to is my own personal [experience]. It was a different era of tabloid journalism and scrutiny, and we lived in a monoculture. There weren’t fringe people with opinions on the internet, and it was one media and pretty unanimous news that we were all digesting. So if there was a public persona of you, that was pretty much the [only] public persona of you, and it was very difficult to have a say in that. It’s such a different culture now that I don’t think it exists in the same way. I think that if I was treated the way that I was then, I would have a much louder voice or means to come back at it.

But in terms of [playing] the actresses, I don’t know. I think it’s less that I’m seeking out these roles and more that those are the roles that people see me as, probably because a famous actress is part of my identity in a way [but] I don’t feel is part of me. I feel like an actor who’s not very famous — and a mom. But it’s quite funny to perhaps send myself up by playing heightened versions of whatever I imagine people might assume that to be, maybe. Although I have played a lot of actresses — and I can’t even remember them all now — I’ve also played a lot of non-actresses, so it feels like there’s variety for me.

You and Carla are fundamentally different people, but I would imagine you also know what it feels like to not be able to leave your own house or to live in a gilded cage because of the paparazzi. Even though you have moved past that chapter of your life, do those feelings ever come up when you are playing these women? Or are you always able to separate your own experiences from the characters you play?

No, I feel like when I’m put actually in the circumstances of getting through a pack [of people] into a car, my heart starts racing. I do have some body memory of it, even though I know it’s pretend. That’s your job, I think, as an actor. It’s to summon things or have them just appear for you in this instance because your past experience is what you can draw on. But I think if I was to get another script of a famous actress, I’d probably not do it, unless she was really different.

Unless she was even more awful than Carla?

Yeah, exactly. (Laughs.)

***

All episodes of War are now streaming on HBO Max in the U.S. and Sky NOW in the U.K.

11jhp5h.title: GTA 6 Crosstown Traffic walkthrough
11jhp5h.content: Here’s how to complete Crosstown Traffic in GTA 6.The mission, which is given by your new contact Raul, splits the couple across Vice City. While Jason follows a convoy of boats along the river on a motorbike, Lucia boards a metro overground train to get close to one of the gang’s associates.Here’s everything you need to know about completing Crosstown Traffic in GTA 6, including what rewards you’ll get at the end of it.Are you looking for more GTA 6 guides? Then check out our GTA 6 Guide Hub.Guides: If you're playing Grand Theft Auto 6, make sure to check out our complete walkthrough hub, featuring beginner tips, navigation experience explained, GTA 6 cheats, and more.GTA 6 Crosstown Traffic walkthroughOnce you’ve received the phonecall from Raul, you can start the mission from either of two locations:Starting as Lucia: Head to the Courtyard Bar in Stockyard to meet Raul.Starting as Jason: Visit the boatyard in La Perle to meet Karim.It doesn’t matter which character you choose. Both starting locations lead into the same mission, with the story switching between Lucia and Jason as the operation unfolds. This also doesn’t impact what rewards you get, or any choices in the mission.The mission is split into several objectives, alternating between Lucia’s metro operation and Jason’s pursuit of the boat convoy. The game swaps you between the two automatically, so you don’t need to keep an eye on this.Follow the boatsAfter the opening cutscene, you’ll take control of Jason, who is riding a motorbike along the riverbank.Your objective is to follow the boats carrying the shipment. Stick to the dirt paths alongside the river and keep the boats in sight as you follow it through Vice City. If you let them get away, or destroy the bike by falling into the water, the mission will end.As long as you keep up with them, you’ll be fine. You can’t take them down here or anything like that, you’re just tailing them until the game automatically swaps to the next portion with Lucia.Eventually, Jason will reach the drop-off point and the game will switch to Lucia.Catch the MetroLucia’s part of the mission begins with her missing the train.You’ll need to catch up with it before it gets too far away. Sprint underneath the elevated railway tracks, following the route marked on your minimap. You can jump into a car (or in our case use one of the Lime scooter-style Escooters that are sitting around) to make it to the next metro station.If you miss the train’s departure, it may be possible to board it at the next station, but it’s also possible the mission will fail for you getting too far from the gang.   Look for the stairs leading up to the next metro station. Once you reach the platform, board the train.It’s worth moving quickly during this section, as wasting time can make it harder to catch up with the train.Confront the Guardia Brothers memberOnce aboard the metro, make your way towards the front carriage to find the Guardia Brothers member.Approach the man and intimidate him. Lucia will force him to the floor, allowing you to pressure him into cooperating. You’ll then need to take his phone and make him place a call to the boat couriers. Either of the conversation prompts works here, as he will eventually make the call.With the call made, Jason can move in on the shipment.Hijack the boatThe game automatically switches back to Jason, who finds himself under attack from gang members on the dock.Take out the two armed baddies before getting back on the motorcycle. Follow the boats along the river, keeping an eye out for Karim’s directions. When he tells you to turn right at the bridge, follow his instructions.Continue along the route until you reach a ramp that launches Jason onto one of the boats. This part is scripted so you just need to get into a good enough position that the game will throw you aboard.Once aboard, deal with the enemy crew. When you’re close enough, jump across to the boat carrying the shipment.With the boat under your control, the operation moves into its next part of the mission as Lucia.Stop the trainYou’ll switch back to Lucia, who is still aboard the metro.At this point, more gang members will appear and attack her. Take them down using melee attacks. Once the enemies have been dealt with, make your way towards the back of the train.Look for the emergency Stop button and interact with it before the train reaches the next station.This completes Lucia’s part of the mission. The game now switches back to Jason.Escape the Coast GuardThe final section of Crosstown Traffic sees Lucia join Jason aboard the stolen boat.You’ll now need to defend the shipment against waves of pursuing enemies, including gang members on jetskis, armed boats and eventually the Coast Guard.Before the firefight gets underway, check the rear seats of the boat. You’ll find an assault rifle and body armour that will make the upcoming battle considerably easier. You’ll have unlimited ammo in this section, so don’t worry about that, though you’ll still have to reload after every 30 bullets.Focus on the drivers of the pursuing boats and jetskis. Taking out the person controlling a vehicle will cause it to crash, making this a much more effective strategy than repeatedly shooting at the vehicles themselves. You can shoot the boats to disable them, but this takes way longer than a well-placed Focus Mode headshot.Eventually, a Coast Guard helicopter will join the pursuit. Rather than wasting ammunition firing at its body, aim through the front windshield and take out the pilot.Keep defending the boat until you get a scripted sequence with Karim droping containers from a bridge. This brings the playable part of Crosstown Traffic to an end.With the shipment secured, the mission concludes.GTA 6 Crosstown Traffic mission rewardsCompleting Crosstown Traffic rewards you with $3,000 cash.That’s everything you need to know about Crosstown Traffic from GTA 6.
